title: Student-teachers’ pedagogical beliefs: learner-centred or teacher-centred when using ICT in the science classroom?
extended_summary:
This exploratory case study examines whether four PGCE student-teachers’ stated pedagogical beliefs aligned with their actual classroom practice when they used ICT for teaching science. The paper is motivated by the common theory-practice gap in teacher education: student-teachers may espouse constructivist, learner-centred views while enacting more teacher-centred, instructivist lessons.

The study investigated how four South African PGCE students used ICT and what influenced those uses. Data sources included a teacher belief system (TBS) tool, drawing prompts followed by interviews, an open-ended questionnaire, lesson plans, assessment feedback forms, short emailed summaries of ICT use, and interviews with the Science Method lecturer and mentor teacher. The participants were Science/Mathematics student-teachers completing school-based learning at a rural school in the Eastern Cape, South Africa. They had grown up in under-resourced township schools with little or no ICT access.

Findings suggest a mismatch between espoused beliefs and classroom enactment. Although the participants described constructivist and learner-centred beliefs, their ICT use was mostly teacher-centred: PowerPoint, YouTube videos, simulations, and software were used primarily to present content, demonstrate experiments, explain procedures, and manage the lesson flow. Some learner-centred elements appeared, such as group work, question-and-answer exchanges, discussion, and opportunities for reflection, but these were limited. The paper concludes that these student-teachers need stronger support, modelling, and opportunities to design and enact learner-centred ICT lessons; it also highlights how prior schooling, tertiary experiences, and lecturer modelling shaped their practice.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a qualitative exploratory case study with four student-teachers, triangulated with mentor/lecturer feedback. It provides rich practice-level evidence but does not estimate causal effects or generalizable outcome impacts.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper suggests modest practical benefits in classroom efficiency and engagement, but it reports no measured learning gains and emphasizes that implementation remained mostly teacher-centred. The impact on student outcomes is therefore unclear and limited.

interventions.use_case: Student-teachers used ICT for science instruction via PowerPoint slides, pre-downloaded YouTube videos, simulations, and computer-assisted learning software (e.g. CAMI maths/science, Khan maths/science) to present content, demonstrate experiments, and support explanations when lab equipment was unavailable.

Science and mathematics simulations were used to illustrate concepts such as electricity circuits and velocity, allowing learners to observe processes that could not easily be done as live practicals.

finding.finding_summary: The paper does not test learning gains, but it provides qualitative evidence that ICT use in science lessons supported conceptual explanation, demonstration of experiments, and access to otherwise unavailable practical experiences. At the same time, the enactment was largely teacher-centred, limiting opportunities for learner discovery and scientific inquiry even when videos, simulations, or group work were used.
finding.measure: Qualitative analysis of lesson plans, interviews, drawings, assessor feedback, and teacher reflections on science lesson practice

finding.finding_summary: The student-teachers reported and were observed to use some questioning, discussion, and group work, which could support collaboration and engagement, but these elements were limited and inconsistent. Overall, ICT lessons were still described by supervisors as largely instructivist, with only small movement toward learner-centred participation.
finding.measure: Observations and reflective accounts of questioning, discussion, and group work during ICT-supported science lessons

finding.finding_summary: Participants believed ICT could make lessons more engaging and less intimidating for learners, and one participant explicitly described a 'humanizing pedagogy' intended to reduce fear and invite questions. However, the overall classroom enactment still showed teacher control and limited learner voice, so the socio-emotional benefits were partial rather than consistent.
finding.measure: Qualitative reports of learner engagement, comfort, and willingness to ask questions in ICT-supported lessons

finding.finding_summary: Participants reported that PowerPoint, videos, and pre-downloaded materials saved lesson time and reduced the need to redraw diagrams or conduct unavailable experiments. These tools were used as substitutes for scarce resources and to streamline presentation, suggesting improved instructional efficiency rather than measured learning gains.
finding.measure: Qualitative reports of teaching time saved and substitution for scarce apparatus/resources
